extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, referees, and scholars interested in peer-review processes (especially in behavioral and social sciences)
extracted.subtask_description: Discussion and guidance on journal peer-review procedures: referee selection, anonymity, monitoring, rating forms, editorial decisions, and possible reforms to improve reliability and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior/publication & copyright compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect potential breach of copyright because of prior or simultaneous publication elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reviewers should check whether submissions have been published or accepted elsewhere; multiple publication can be discovered late (even after acceptance). Copyright release forms are clear about prior publication; republication may be acceptable only under special, previously agreed-upon circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: International representation in referee selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate to the discipline, include international referees and commentators; internationality can be intrinsic (e.g., anthropology) or extrinsic in other sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select reviewers based on area of expertise rather than geographic area unless cross-cultural or area-specific knowledge is required. Make special effort to include European, Eastern European, and Far Eastern contributions where appropriate; ensure associateship, authorship, commentatorship, and subscribership are internationally representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal number of referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a sample of 5-8 referees (BBS practice) rather than the conventional 1-3 or extremely large panels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5-8 is an improvement over 1-3; larger samples may increase noise, reduce the chance a manuscript can be revised to everyone's satisfaction, and introduce undesirable committee-writing features. A third coin toss analogy: 3 referees give a tiebreaker; precontacting raises response rate to near 100%, making smaller samples effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precontacting referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Precontact referees (e.g., by telephone) to ascertain willingness to referee and ability to meet deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precontacting yields near-100% response rates and improves turnaround. Time and telephone costs may constrain precontacting (often to domestic referees), but when foreign referees are clearly optimal, send manuscripts even if not precontacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative referee selection via computer-assisted techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Use computer-assisted referee selection (search current literature and associate lists) to find qualified specialists and create a fair, representative sample of referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computer search of a large reviewer file reduces opportunities for editorial bias by identifying referees the editor does not personally know; can find reviewers with combinations of specialties (e.g., 'Africa' + 'urban'), improving match quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of foreign referees despite precontact constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: When particular foreign referees would be optimal, include them by sending a copy of the manuscript even if precontacting is not feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time and cost pressures may limit precontacting to domestic reviewers; nevertheless, foreign experts should be included when their expertise is critical—they can be sent manuscripts without precontacting to supplement the domestic quota.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-blind review with optional referee anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: BBS uses a non-blind procedure with optional referee anonymity: authors are nonanonymous; referees may be anonymous to protect freedom of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonanonymity of authors has not proven problematic for BBS; optional anonymity for referees aims to ensure freedom of judgment, but anonymity has trade-offs (e.g., can encourage punitive behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor evaluation of referee reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should evaluate each referee's report (checklist plus written text) relative to other reports and the manuscript itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor assessment is part of referee accountability; editorial ratings can be used along with author and referee data in ongoing statistical studies to monitor review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author ratings of referee reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are asked to rate each referee report in terms of how favorable and how useful they find it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author ratings supplement editorial evaluation and provide data for cumulative monitoring of referee and commentator performance; allows matched-guise comparisons between anonymous referee reports and open commentaries by the same individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cumulative monitoring of referee performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically monitor referee performance using multiple indicators: ratings, willingness, timeliness, and editorial evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain cumulative records to inform future referee selection and to study relations among anonymity, referee ratings, and other performance metrics; use statistical studies to report findings and improve processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-assisted reviewer database
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a large, computer-based file of potential referees to reduce delays and some bias in reviewer selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Populate the file from department guides, published authors, and referrals; use a text editor or database to locate reviewers by any combination of specialties. This approach reduced review times to under two months in Bernard's experience and makes it easy to find alternates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral selection criteria for reviewer databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer reviewer lists based on actual publication behavior (published in last 5-6 years) rather than self-reported expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A behaviorally based reviewer file (journals, books, theses) avoids the major flaw of self-report systems; disciplines or associations might develop systems to produce and update such files and offer subfiles to subscribing journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized reviewer master file / service
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a central service that produces and updates a master file of reviewers for major scientific areas (e.g., social and behavioral sciences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals could subscribe and pay for subfiles in particular areas; the cost is small and benefits (reduced delay, reduced bias) are substantial. Today, microcomputers can handle reviewer files for many journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeouts and replacement referees
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reviewer fails to respond within 3-4 weeks, send the manuscript to alternative referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to replace nonresponders promptly; the computer/database can rapidly locate alternates and maintain timely review flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation and continuing commentary as review mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Solicit commentaries widely (e.g., 50+) and use Continuing Commentary sections to permit further rounds of unsolicited commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open peer commentary can draw a wide range of participants and can encourage junior authors by providing useful advice even when manuscripts are not accepted for full treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of journal space scarcity on review decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: High rejection rates often reflect scarcity of space rather than pure quality concerns; referees may feel compelled to reject most submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When acceptance rates must match limited space, referees document reasons for rejection; comparisons across fields should consider differences in available publication space and resulting acceptance pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical limits on deceptive research of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise caution about using deception in studies of peer review (e.g., resubmitting altered published papers), weighing benefits versus distress caused to editors and reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify deceptive methods only if benefits outweigh costs and if such results cannot be obtained otherwise; P & C's deceptive resubmissions are critiqued for limited generalizability and ethical concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliation status (academic vs nonacademic) bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing an author's affiliation (from a prestigious university to an unknown nonacademic institution) may affect referees' judgments beyond mere prestige differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bias may result from perceived nonacademic origin as much as from lower prestige; studies interpreting affiliation effects should distinguish academic/nonacademic status from prestige alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for peer-review errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms to rectify mistakes include appeal panels, higher tribunals, open peer commentary, improved selection procedures, standard rating forms, and referee reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices may be helpful in some cases but are not panaceas; process remedies must be complemented by attention to disciplinary content and structure to address deeper problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author responses prior to editorial decision (dialectical review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Afford authors an opportunity to reply to reviews before the editor makes a decision, creating a dialectical review-and-recourse process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a procedure can help recognize referees for valuable work, restore accountability, and may improve fairness by letting authors clarify misunderstandings prior to acceptance/rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish referee identities for accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove referee anonymity and append to the published article the names of referees who recommended publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This could increase accountability and communal spirit, but may deter junior reviewers (fear of reprisal) and bias participation toward established scientists who support the status quo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associate editors' role and status-based peer definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Scrutinize how referees are selected: assess the roles of associate editors and whether authors' status and institutional affiliations define who their 'peers' are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection politics and underlying epistemologies influence reviewer choice; transparency and improved selection procedures can mitigate status-driven biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript attribute rating form items
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard rater form (example from Journal of Abnormal Psychology) includes: (1) probable reader interest, (2) importance of contribution, (3) attention to relevant literature, (4) research design, (5) data analysis, (6) style and organization, (7) succinctness — with specified scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms may use 4- or 10-point scales and include item-specific instructions (e.g., disregard design for case reports). Cicchetti reports reviewers agree on relative weighting: importance and research design are most relevant; succinctness least relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating forms may not improve interrater reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evidence suggests rating forms and training may not increase interreferee agreement and can sometimes lower agreement compared to unstructured reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cicchetti & Eron found lower agreement (R intraclass = .15) with a 7-item form versus higher agreement (R(I) = .21) without the form; training reviewers to map checklist items to publishability may be futile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude reviewers with repeated legitimate complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Cease calling upon reviewers who have received repeated legitimate complaints about their performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing consistently problematic reviewers is one proposed antidote to improve review quality and protect authors from poor or biased evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage creative disagreement among referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase the role of 'creative disagreement' to enrich evaluation and avoid groupthink.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diverse, thoughtful disagreement can surface different perspectives and reduce the chance of collective error; editorial systems should value constructive dissent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between reliability and validity in review decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: High interreferee reliability (agreement) does not guarantee validity — referees may unanimously accept flawed research that is later invalidated by specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should be aware that consensus among referees can still produce invalid decisions; systems must seek both reliable and valid evaluations (e.g., include domain experts who can detect fatal flaws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diverse reasoning behind similar recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees may agree on a recommendation (accept/reject/revise) for entirely different and sometimes conflicting reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should examine not just the recommendation but the underlying reasons; similar recommendations that rest on different critiques require careful editorial synthesis to avoid misinformed decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of reviewer disclosure on reviewer pool composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring reviewer disclosure may discourage junior reviewers and result in an excess of established referees who may have a stake in maintaining the status quo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should balance accountability benefits from disclosure with potential deterrent effects on participation by less-established scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial self-awareness of potential for punitive selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must recognize they can intentionally (or unintentionally) select reviewers who will 'clobber' a manuscript; systems should reduce opportunities for punitive or biased selections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a large, impersonal reviewer database helps mitigate but does not eliminate editorial prejudice; ongoing monitoring and transparency can reduce misuse.
